Urban spaces have been interpreted and been transformed due to many factors , whether it be economical ,social, or religious factors. One of the places that was impacted by some of these factors was the Tawantinsuyu, home of the Incas in Cuzco and is also known as the Realm of the Four Quarters. Many of the transformations of its urban space can be attributed to the structure that it upholds as well as the monuments that are placed throughout the empire.. This report will analyze the systems that contribute to how the inhabitants organize themselves when in the empires and how the physical structures affect ceremonies and contribute to the urban landscape.
	We first want to showcase how the name of the Realm of the Four Quarters came to be. As a way to divide responsibilities among various households, they divided the empire into four quarters or suyus which intersect at the center of the Cuzco. As Alan Kolata mentioned in the article  “In the Realm of the Four Quarters” , he mentioned that with this choice of splitting the empire into four quarters enabled the households in charge to have local autonomy as they didn’t have to intrude on the villages and gave permission for leaders to hold their taxes.
	The zeq’e system , as defined in the chapter title “The Inca Capital Cuzco as the Model of an Imperial Cultural Landscape '', comprises forty-one imaginary lines that radiate out from the Temple of the Sun , or Qorikancha, into Cuzco and beyond. They are split between the four suyus : Chinchaysuyu, Antisuyu, and Kollasuyu contain nine zeq’es each as the last quarter, Kuntisuyu, has the rest, which is fourteen.  Along these imaginary lines were the placing of shrines or wak’as, for a total of 328, including springs, tombs, hills, and standing stones. But all the zeq’e were revered by the families as Father Bernabe Cobo,author of the Historia del Neuvo Mundo, quoted , “ Each ceque was the responsibility of the kinship units and families of the city of Cuzco, from within which came the attendants  and servants who cared for the guacas of their ceque and saw to offering the established sacrifices at the proper times.”  The families usually are part of the Cuzco lineage that each maintained several wak’as at a time. They also serve appropriate sacrifices at certain times during ceremonies. It really goes to support this statement made by Jean- Pierre Protzen and John Howland Rowe, two of many writers in the published work Streets : Critical Perspective on Public Space where they stated “It is obvious that the “zeq’e system did not influence the general physical structure of Cuzco: nothing in the city’s layout would lead one to suspect a radial pattern. Yet the zeq’e system must have played an important role in how the city’s residents perceived and understood its spatial organization, and influenced the way they oriented themselves in it.”

In Victoria Siu’s book chapter “Experiencing the Garden of Perfect Brightness (Yuanming Yuan),” it is evidently clear that religion heavily impacted the design of the Garden of Perfect Brightness, as well as its use in respects to the Lantern Festival. For one thing, within the design of the Garden of Perfect Brightness, it included the Sravasti Complex, a large Buddhist temple at 139,500 square feet. Infact, its name “Sravasti” was inspired by India's Sravasti town, most recognized for its Buddhist history. In addition, Sravasti temple complex was structurally designed to emphasize a high degree of importance. For example, the Sravasti temple included “Chinese-style northsouth axis, double walls, encircling protective stream, and position amid several important complexes”, (pg. 12). Furthermore, the temple’s interior design also captivates the significant influence religion holds within the Garden of Perfect Brightness, as it was filled with thousands of Buddhist religious images, as well as the statue of the God of War. In essence, this Sravasti Complex was solely intended for Buddhist rituals and the worship of gods. Therefore, during the Lantern Festival, the Qianlong emperor used this temple to perform evening rituals. Moreover, similar to many of the other temples in the Garden of Perfect Brightness, the Ancestral Shrine located in the Palace of Peaceful Protection Complex, was also designed for worshipping specifically for Confucianism ceremonies during the Lantern Festival. This explains why the Ancestral Shrine was depicted to be extremely spacious including vast reception halls, surrounded by tall hills, and with its roof glazed or containing enamel tiles. All in all, both the Ancestral Shrine and Sravasti Complex are prime examples of such impacts that religion and ancestral worshiping has had on the Garden of Perfect Brightness.
